title: Bound, by choice
hookLine: Hanuman beats every champion Lanka sends, until a god's weapon binds him, and the enemy's own ropes undo it
carry: shraddha: trust given whole, not halfway

cards: Ravana keeps raising the stakes. After the first wave falls, he sends Jambumali, a fierce warrior. Then seven sons of his ministers, in shining chariots.

Then five of his generals. Each time the same news comes back to the palace: the monkey is still on the gate. Then Ravana sends his own young son, Aksha, and Valmiki pauses the fighting to let Hanuman look at the boy.

teach.b: Hanuman admires Aksha; Valmiki tells us so. The boy is brave and skilled, radiant like the young sun, and Hanuman is reluctant to kill one so young.
But Aksha's arrows keep coming, and he decides an enemy this strong can't be ignored. The epic doesn't hide the cost. Now Ravana sends his son Indrajit, whose name means conqueror of Indra.
Their duel is long, and neither can wound the other.
So Indrajit reaches for the weapon of Brahma, the Brahmastra, and binds Hanuman with it. Hanuman falls. And he knows this weapon: by Brahma's own blessing, it can hold him only a short while.

He chooses to stay down, out of respect for Brahma, and because it serves his purpose: to be brought before Ravana. Then comes the detail teachers love. The rakshasas aren't content to leave him in the god's weapon.

teach.h: ROPES ADDED; THE WEAPON LETS GO.
teach.b: They tie him with ropes and bark of their own, and Valmiki says the Brahmastra lets go the moment other bonds are added. Indrajit despairs; his own soldiers have undone his weapon.

Some devotional teachers read this as a lesson in shraddha, faith given whole: a sacred bond doesn't share the job with doubt. On that reading, the scene shows two kinds of trust. The rakshasas hedge, and lose their hold.
Hanuman honors the god and trusts the moment to carry him where Rama needs him. He lets them drag him through the streets into the hall where Ravana sits.

how: Hanuman bound by Indrajit's Brahmastra appears in recitations and dance-dramas, and some teachers of the Sundara Kanda use the ropes that undo the divine weapon to talk about shraddha, wholehearted faith.

games.q: you're one of Ravana's guards. Indrajit's divine weapon already holds the monkey, but you don't quite trust it. you add your own ropes. what happens?
games.why: Valmiki says the Brahmastra releases its hold once other bonds are added. some teachers read it as shraddha: a sacred bond doesn't share the job with doubt.

practice: If you pray or do aarti, offer one prayer today with nothing else in your hands: no phone, no list running, the whole of you for one minute.
If you don't pray, give one thing your full trust and attention for a minute, a conversation, a meal, a person, without hedging. Breathe, and notice how different whole feels from halfway.

wordCard.voice: The fight. Wave after wave, young Aksha, then Indrajit's Brahmastra, which Hanuman honors though he could escape, until the rakshasas' own ropes undo it.

orig.note: Sanskrit brahmāstra: brahma, the creator, and astra, a missile or divine weapon.

carryVoice: Your line: shraddha: trust given whole, not halfway. Tomorrow, the throne room. Day six hundred twenty-seven, done.
